utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and listening and watching to us. We have a delayed start because of some transportation problems of the Dutch police, as I was told. At the outset, I would like to raise two procedural matters. The first is an oral decision. The Chamber wishes to return to the pending issue concerning the admission into evidence of document 65 ter 03484, an intercepted communication dated 19th of July, 1995, between a certain person named X and Milovanovic. This intercept was used by the Prosecution during its re-examination of the witness Erin Gallagher last Friday the 29th of October. The Chamber reviewed this intercept, the witness's testimony as a whole, as well as the examination of both parties. The majority, with Judge Nyambe dissenting, is satisfied that it is prima facie relevant and probative under Rule 89(C) of our Rules of Procedure and evidence and that sufficient indicia of reliability exist. Therefore, the majority decides the admit this document 65 ter 03484 into evidence. Judge Nyambe dissents for the reason that although the intercept may be prima facie relevant, she is of the view that the accused's objections should be sustained for the reasons stated by the accused. Additionally, this intercept should be formally tendered by the Prosecution through the person who produced or transcribed it and not a secondary witness. In her view, the intercept may be marked MFI until such time that the Prosecution would tender it through the appropriate witness. Should the Prosecution fail to produce the witness who transcribed the intercept, the Chamber, in accordance with the Rules of the Tribunal, will still have the possibility to call this witness as a Chamber witness. That was the reasoning, the oral ruling. I would like to ask the Prosecution if there is a translation of this intercept already available in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. We do have an English translation and a -- well, obviously, the B/C/S already exists, but we do have an English translation which should be uploaded into e-court soon for that, if -- it should be on its way, if not already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That may be checked immediately but if that is not possible, we will mark this document for identification pending translation. The second matter is the request of the OTP for additional time to compile a list of exhibits in relation to the Rule 92 bis decision of July -- 7th of July of this year. The Chamber reviewed the arguments and the information given by the Prosecution in the meantime and is giving now an additional time until the 17th of December to comply with the -- the order of the Chamber. If there is nothing else -- Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My microphone seems particularly powerful today. I'll stand back a little bit. Just to let you know, Your Honours, by the end of this week we should have completed approximately ten of those 92 bis packages that are the subject of the ruling Your Honour just issued, so we are moving forward and we should be able to meet that dead-line for which we thank the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness should be brought in, please. In the meantime, I would like to ask the Prosecution about the arrangements with the Dutch translator, interpreter. We are not sure if we can finish with this witness today. What are the arrangements?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it appears that we will not be able to proceed tomorrow. The language folks here tried very hard to secure some Dutch interpreters for tomorrow, but we were not successful in that. My understanding from speaking with the Defence is that they will need more time than is available today, so unfortunately, I think, unless we finish today, we will have to reschedule for a date in the future to bring Colonel Egbers back. It's unfortunate, but finding Dutch translators, surprisingly enough, is difficult to do in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court Usher is asked to assist the witness with the chair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you help me with the chair? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And please tell me, is it high enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, good afternoon again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge. May there be peace in this house. I greet everybody present, especially the witness, and I wish that today's proceedings conclude in keeping with God's will and not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall presume where we left off yesterday. Yesterday we left off where you were saying on the first page, you were describing a situation, and I am quoting. That is the last paragraph of page 2 of document 1145.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can that be brought up on the screen. It is Exhibit P1145, page 3 in the Serbian language. In actual fact it is page 2 in the Serbian language, the last paragraph which is the fourth one. And it is page 3, the first paragraph in the English version. Thank you. We now see in English -- we should be seeing page 3 in English, the first paragraph, and page 2, paragraph 4 in the Serbian version, lines 9, 10, and 11. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a situation where you state, describe, what you saw, and I should like to quote it but I still cannot see it on the screen. You can but I cannot -- well, now, yes. Well, we now cannot see the English: "There were between eight and ten Muslims there. At a certain point they -- at a certain point we were shot at by a tank or artillery coming from a south-easterly direction. They fired in succession. "The Bosnian Serbian soldiers might have been shooting at the Muslim fighters. The attack took place about five or ten metres away." Then you go on to say that: "The Muslim commander was seriously wounded in the shooting and was hit by a piece of shrapnel in his tarmac, and two of the Muslims were slightly wounded, one got a shrapnel in his neck and the other in his arm." Please be so kind as to clarify this, you say they fired in succession?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just -- we all have the document in front of us, but just for the sake of the transcript, I think General Tolimir misread the portion. It's not two of the Muslims were slightly wounded, but "two of my men," that is, UN peacekeepers, were slightly wounded, just so there is no confusion if one is reading the record later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer, for correcting the transcript. The last sentence which I quoted was: "Two of my men were slightly wounded, one got a shrapnel in his neck and the other in his arm." And that's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you this: In this paragraph which I read out, you said that there was firing in succession. Do you think that that was fire exchanged between you and the Serbs or the Serbs and the Muslims? What exactly did you refer to when you say there was firing in succession?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I intend to describe there is that we were at a spot that was clearly visible to everybody, also for the crew of a Serb tank that was firing in our direction. As for the question of whether I was 100 per cent certain that the shooting was at me and at my people or whether the shooting was at the Bosnian warriors in our surrounding, I can't tell you exactly with respect to that moment. The tank was firing at us, the grenades hit, and we took up a different position. At the time, I wasn't certain whether they were shooting at us or at the Muslim warriors. This became clear only later when the route to the point where we positioned ourselves concealed the -- was also shot at, but at that other moment I was not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this part which I quoted, you said that the Muslims were 5 metres away from you. Was the gunner on the Serbian army's tank able to discern from what point he was being fired at from the 5 metres' point away from you or from your firing ordinance, from your weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I didn't object yesterday when General Tolimir made this misstatement, but -- and we have the statement in front of us. But, again, for the record, that is not what the statement says. That is a misstatement. The Muslim fighters were clearly positioned at a different distance which is recorded here, and General Tolimir needs to cite the paragraph correctly in his questions and not misstate the clear language of the paragraph. I understand Colonel Egbers was there and he's an experienced officer, but we simply need to make sure that this transcript is accurate and not being misstated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer, for your assistance. Thank you, Presiding Judge. Can we now look at page 3, second line. Page 3, first paragraph, second line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "The attack took place about 5 or 10 metres away from where we were."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And where is it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where is this part in the English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is in the first paragraph on the page which is now on the screen at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, that is misstating what is clearly in the paragraph. He did this yesterday, and Colonel Egbers corrected him yesterday as well. Colonel Egbers was clear that the Muslims were at a position, as you can see in the statement, 40 metres to the north-west. He said again yesterday that they were perhaps 50 to 60 metres from there and that the shells were landing at that distance that's indicated here. The reference to the attack is, as Colonel Egbers said yesterday, where the shells landed, not where the Muslims were. This is the third time that General Tolimir is trying to imply that the Muslims had positioned themselves 5 metres from the DutchBat position which is clearly not the case. Again, it is misrepresenting both what's in the statement, it's misrepresenting what Colonel Egbers clearly clarified yesterday. That is why I am making this objection, because we cannot have this transcript distorted by misstatements of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, perhaps you can help us. I am also referring to the sentence: "The attack took place about 5 or 10 metres away." What does that mean in your understanding? Could you please explain it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a distance between the Dutch and the Bosnian warriors. That distance was, say, 50 metres. The hits that injured us were 5 to 10 metres away, so the shells fell very close to our vehicles but because there were Bosnian warriors 50 metres away, I was unable to say that the firing was only at me. That's why I wrote it down and explained it this way, so the attack was directed at my position and the Bosnian warriors were 50 metres away from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And when you say "Bosnian warriors," you are referring to Bosnian Muslim fighters; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were indeed men dressed in civilian attire armed with rifles pertaining to the Muslim group within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me this: Can a soldier aboard a Serbian tank know whether he was being shot at by the Muslim positions or by you? Was he suppose or was he able to exactly determine the firing line in order to be able to return fire, meaning the firing line from which shots came at him?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taught that such a tank cannot fire further than about 1500 metres, direct fire, but this Serb tank targeted its barrel upward and was able to fire fairly accurately at our location. I am not sure how good the Serb tank crew was, but the shells hit very close to us. I am not sure whether it was his intention to hit us or the Muslims, the only thing I can tell you is that the shells landed 5 to 10 metres away from our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were not hit directly by this tank shell which fell a few metres away from you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not personally hit directly, but several soldiers sustained minor injuries. All I had was damage to my hearing. We were very lucky that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So I got as part of the answer: You were not directly hit, but how far was the Serbian tank which fired this shell which landed near you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a previous testimony, I stated about the Serbian tank. It was certainly a few kilometres away from my position near an altitude of, off the top of my head, on the map known as 757, 15 years ago. The tank was in that area and it was not directly emitting fire, but the barrel of the tank was pointing upward so that an artillery fire was emitted by the tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to take you back to your last question, page 10, line 1. You said, and that was the interpretation we received: "So I got as part of the answer: You were not directly hit." Were you at this question referring to Mr. Egbers personally and only to him or to the UNPROFOR, the DutchBat soldiers present at this spot?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please clarify for us: Were UNPROFOR soldiers then in the vehicle in which you were, and was that vehicle hit at that point by the shell which was fired from Serbian position, from a tank on Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness said: "I was not personally hit directly, but several soldiers sustained minor injuries. All I had was damage to my hearing." You got the answer that some of the soldiers were, indeed, hit, and sustained injured. I just wanted to make clear because in your next question you said: "... you were not injured directly." This can only refer to the witness personally and not to the other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Earlier I noticed, and you can correct me, that the shell landed by you, near you. This shell from the tank. Did it land among the soldiers, UNPROFOR soldiers, on the vehicle or on the ground around you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armoured vehicles were not hit directly, only a bit of shrapnel from the grenade hit them. The Muslim warriors did not have the protection of armoured vehicles, and some of them were seriously injured. We sustained only minor damage, the UNPROFOR soldiers sustained minor injuries. Muslim warriors sustained serious injuries. We had armoured vehicles, APCs, they did not have those. Does this answer your question sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, this is a sufficient answer. Tell me, from -- did you see the wounded Muslims from your vehicle or did you get off the vehicle in order to establish what wounds the Muslims had sustained?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the injuries only later on. When the shooting started, everybody fled. We drove away as quickly as possible. Later, when the firing stopped and we returned to the original position, I saw the injuries among the Muslim warriors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 2 on page 3, in Serbian, you first say that you took up positions about 400 metres further on. What does this "further on" refer to, towards the Serbian positions or in some other direction? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was on a road with two 180 [Realtime transcript read in error "280"] degree turns. The road from Srebrenica to OP Alpha. I stood 400 metres further down protected in the -- proceeded in the direction of Srebrenica outside the view of the tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a quick correction. I don't think there will be any dispute about this. In the witness's answer, at page 12, line 6, it reads: "I was on a road with 280 degree turns." I think he said "two 180 degree turns," not "280 degree turns." So I think that needs to be corrected and we can perhaps confirm with the witness, but I am pretty sure we all heard two 180 degree turns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Perhaps if the General has a map, I could point it out to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There is no need to belabour this point. Please be so kind as to take a look at page 3, paragraph 2, line 5 where then you say: "I then received an order to support the other four vehicles in Srebrenica. We left our positions and the Muslim fighters started shooting at us. About 30 metres below the arm of the gunner, a bullet hit the turret of our vehicle. Metal splinters flew into his arm. I think that the Muslim fighters shot at us out of fear because they thought that we were abandoning them." Are you able -- can you see this text in the English version which I've just quoted?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to what you told me. I know exactly what you are talking about, but I don't know exactly what I have in front of me because I don't see any line or page numbers. But I understand it should be all the way at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the left side of the screen. One moment, Mr. Tolimir. It is on the left side of the screen, second paragraph, and the first half of the second paragraph. You see there a small sign.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it clearly. Do you have a question about this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I do have a question for you: Did you return fire when Muslims had opened fire on you, representatives of UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I did not fire back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a moment when you returned fire and opened fire on the Muslims who had shot at you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were fired at already when we were driving toward the city of Srebrenica, and only 100 metres after we were out of the view of the warriors did I hear that the gunner had been injured. I did not return to become involved in the exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at page 3, paragraph 3, line 1. It is below the paragraph that is now marked for you. You say: "In Srebrenica, I saw many armed Muslims." The cursor is next to that paragraph now. "I recognised anti-tank weapons RPG 7 and nonautomatic firearms such as the AK-47. Some pointed their weapons at us and through arm movements made it clear to us that we should continue in a southerly direction. We drove to another four vehicles which belonged to us and which were under the command of Captain Hageman. He told me over the radio that he was under fire by the local Muslim combatants and therefore he could not move his vehicles." My question to you, sir, is this: Was that a large-scale attack launched on all members of UNPROFOR on that day, and the day is the 9th? Did all the other soldiers, UNPROFOR soldiers, telephone you just as Colonel Karremans did, that they had come under Muslim fire? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the name Karremans be changed into Hageman. I said Hageman because the witness, in his statement, stated that it was Captain Hageman who had telephoned him to tell him that he had come under fire by the local Muslims. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I drove to the city of Srebrenica I arrived on the square which was filled with people in a state of utter panic. There I saw armed men and while the Bosnian Serbian troops were approaching the city from the south, the Muslims hoped that we would protect them there. They wanted us to drive as much as possible to the south of the square to take up positions there. It was a state of chaos that day. And only one of them might have shot at us and the consequences would have been disastrous. That's why I stood on top of my vehicle to let them know that I needed to pass. Because of the total chaos, several of them ensured that our APCs remained there. They also did this by physically restraining Captain Hageman there and they also tried to restrain my vehicle there, because in their eyes we were the only hope of rescue for them. There was total chaos. There was no attack on our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at paragraph 3, line 5 -- or, rather, line 4 and 5 where it says: "We drove to another four vehicles which belonged to us and which were under the command of Captain Hageman. He told me over the radio that he was under fire, under fire by the local Muslim fighters and therefore he could not move his own vehicles." Thank you. Does this mean that he was physically blocked or was he only blocked by the fire that was opened on them?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression on the square at that time was that there was no shooting at him physically but that he was physically threatened by weapons. If weapons are aimed at you then you receive the message loud and clear. There was no shooting at my vehicle. Captain Hageman told me over the radio that he was stuck and he was afraid to move anywhere because around him there was total panic and people were armed and that's why I drove to him to help him there. These people were in such a state of panic that they even climbed onto my vehicle to keep me there. They wanted us to act to stop the approaching Bosnian Serb tanks. Among all those armed men were women in utter panic. I remember that the day was very, very hot. It was a very hot day and that made a deep impression on all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us very clearly for the record was Captain Hageman exposed to the fire by the local Muslim fighters, as it says here in the text, or not?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody shooting at his vehicle. I do note that he told me that he was threatened and that's why he was stuck and could not take up a different position. That's what I remember. But there was no attack. There was panic, and the population was trying to keep us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I couldn't know that this statement is not correct. Does it mean that this statement is not correct or, at least, this part where Captain Hageman is referred to and what he allegedly told you over the phone? Let's not waste anymore time if the statement is incorrect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I might be able to make a remark about that, even though you're not asking me a question. There it reads that: "He told me over the radio that ...," and that's all there is. I didn't perceive it so I can't determine whether or not that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's not waste any more time on this. Let's now look at the next paragraph, again on page 3, you say: "We stayed there the whole night." The cursor is next to that line now: "The promised air-strike did not take place." And then you say: "A mortar shell hit the ground that night about 10 metres away from the vehicles. Nobody was wounded. The rest of the night was calm." My question is this: You say here the promised air-strike did not take place. Please, who was it who had promised you that there would, indeed, be an air-strike and who was supposed to be the target of that air-strike? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a situation, I speak only with my commander, and my commander promised that there would be air support to ensure that the Bosnian Serb tanks did not advance any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, who your commander was in that case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was under the direct command of Captain Groen, and I communicated with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Captain Groen ever tell you who it was who had told him that the air-strikes would happen and why they didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do now is reason that his commander, the battalion -- the battalion commander would have told him that, but at the time I didn't know who said that and I don't know, to answer the second part of your question, why this didn't happen. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say here, "We stayed there the whole night." Is that night the night between the 9th and the 10th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you already received an order for the so-called Green Alert? Thank you. Green order? Had you already received the green order from your Captain Groen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't give me the direct instructions, but we had to use all means to ensure that the -- that additional advances by the Bosnian Serbs were stopped, and I assumed that air support was essential in this process. We couldn't do anything on the ground with our weapons. At the time, we were on a market square surrounded by houses with hills around us, and behind the hills the Bosnian Serb troops were advancing northward.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, on the 9th in the evening and during the night, was the so-called green order in effect?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case I don't have to remind you what Major Franken said about that as he testified before this Trial Chamber. Let's move on to the follow paragraph. It says here: "The next day, Monday, the 10th of July, 1995, I returned with my group to a safe place in the vicinity of our original location. The forward air control in my vehicle received instructions to prepare for an air-strike again. Once again, nothing happened." Thank you. Could you please tell us, where did you return and where was it that you were instructed to prepare for another air-strike? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was on the market square, I was instructed to return to blocking position 1 because from that position we had a clear view of the south of the enclave where Bosnian tanks and other units were situated. We had to mark our vehicles so that we would be clearly visible from the air. And we were preparing for air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the VRS launch attacks from behind the hill where their tanks were? Were there any attacks on that morning?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't fired at on that day by the Bosnian Serb tanks. I don't remember whether those tanks did fire at other locations at that point. I will speak for myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, on page 18, line 22, you are recorded to having said: "Where the Bosnian tanks and other units were situated." You are referring to Bosnian Serb tanks or what you are talking about? Because on page 19, line 2, you use the term "the Bosnian Serb tanks."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only army with tanks was the Bosnian Serb one, so in this case I use the words Bosnian Serb army, BSA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that in the course of the 10th, fire was not opened on you personally. And now, in paragraph 5, beneath that, it says: "We then got the order to return to our original positions. We were in full view of Bosnian Serbian soldiers. Ten minutes later, we came under tank and mortar attack. Our escape route to a safe place was also under fire. We did, however, manage to return to our safe place. Our vehicles had been hit several times." If we look at this paragraph 5, can you please tell us why were you ordered to return to your original position where we were -- where you were in full view of the Army of Republika Srpska whom you refer to as Bosnian Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe now that conceivably they wanted to be 100 per cent sure that we were being shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't understand you. Did they want to be certain or did they want to expose you to fire? Did they want to have you in full view and is that why they had told you to change your position? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hypothetical line had to be drawn that could not be crossed by Bosnian Serb troops. I was on that hypothetical line and I had to stand there with my vehicles and people, even though I was in full view and was being fired at. At that moment we had to draw a hypothetical line that could not be crossed by the Bosnian Serb army. I was part of that border in full view and that's why I was fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Talking about that hypothetical line that you drew, can you tell us where the Muslims were with regard to that hypothetical line?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims were north of that line; the Bosnian Serb army south of that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How far were the Muslims from that line? Were they armed, could they open fire at you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that many men were already north of this hypothetical line, and perhaps they were preparing to go to Bosnian area, Muslim area, on foot. At that time not many Bosnian soldiers, Bosnian warriors, were in my surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there any Bosnian combatants around you at all around that hypothetical line? Could they open fire, did they open fire at you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What we did see was a Bosnian Serb tank to the south, we heard a bang, we saw smoke, and we saw the hits near us. That was also the information that we transmitted later that day to the F-16s.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How did you receive information about the positions of the Muslim forces and they were -- and where they were at that moment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, all I could do was look around me and did not see many people in my surroundings anymore. So exactly where they were north of the enclave, later on I heard that they were in the surroundings of Observation Post Alpha. But I didn't know that at this time, and all I saw was a tank in the south firing at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How far was Observation Post Alpha away from you, and you say that Muslims were gathered around that observation post, how far was it from you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Again, let's go back to the hypothetical line that you drew. Where did you draw it? Did you draw it somewhere in the centre or did you draw that line somewhere between the Serbs and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That hypothetical line is a line in between the blocking positions. So I could remain standing in blocking position 1. I've testified about this in previous trials and pointed it out on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you drew a hypothetical line on the ground, how did you do it and how did you make it visible to the Serbian forces? Could you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that by making myself visible with my white vehicle. For our own aeroplanes I placed a cloth on top of the vehicle that was visible from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And how did you make the Serbs know that there was, indeed, a hypothetical line there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That must have been agreed at your level between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serb army, not at my level on the ground as lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When was that agreed, do you know anything about that? When was it agreed with the Army of Republika Srpska that there would be a hypothetical line drawn? A hypothetical line would be something as a hypothetical assumption, wouldn't it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told by my own commander that a large aeroplane from the air would be firing at the armoured positions of the Serbs that were located south of the blocking positions. It was not a hypothetical line on the map. It was very easy to draw on the map, and I was part of it, as blocking position number 1 with my white vehicle. Basically, I was a target for everybody and, nonetheless, we stood there to indicate that that was where the line was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the Muslims were about 2 kilometres to the north of that line and that the Serbs were to the south of that line. How far were the Serbs from that line?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims were very close to that line because the entire marketplace at Srebrenica was still filled with people, thousands and thousands of people. The Bosnian Serb tanks drove about a kilometre south of me and were firing at me. Exactly where the largest number of men was exiting the enclave on foot, I couldn't tell you at that time. At that time I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, how far were you from the marketplace where these people, these civilians were in Srebrenica when you were drawing this hypothetical line?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd point that out to you on the map, but I didn't draw a hypothetical line. I had to take up blocking position 1 in the middle of the road with the white vehicle to ensure that it was clearly visible to everybody that UNPROFOR was there and that that line could not be crossed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, as this is the 10th, how could the VRS know that you had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the speaker. Could the speaker please be asked to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch your last question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So, please tell me, how did you shift from a position of someone who had been given the green order to open fire on the Serbs to the position of someone who is going to be neutral and be seen by everyone standing on the road with a white sheet which was to be a signal for the aircraft?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that the Bosnian Serb army was informed that the hypothetical line could not be crossed and that if that happened aeroplanes would be used to neutralise the armoured vehicles of the Bosnian Serbs. If we were to operate in green surroundings, we would not be clearly visible. But in the idea of giving the Bosnian Serbs a final warning not to cross that line, I could understand that, and I basically used my -- I placed my men in the armoured vehicles, basically, as targets on the road as a signal to the Bosnian Serb army so that they would go no further than the positions that we had taken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But I have understood you -- but tell me who informed you that the Bosnian Serb army had been informed that they were not to cross that hypothetical line?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that yet. At high level the battalion commander, or perhaps even higher than that, that was communicated with the Bosnian Serb army. I can't say who did that. All I was told was that it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Colonel Franken play any commanding role in that chain of command? Was he above you in that chain?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Franken was deputy battalion commander at that time and was above Captain Groen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me remind you what Mr. Franken said on the 1st of July, 2010, on the transcript page 3473, line 6. Asked when he had issued the order, he said, and I quote: "That must have been in the evening of the 9th of July." And on page 3453, he explained what the issuance of a green order meant in this way. That is in line 16 to line 19, and I quote: "The rules of engagement that we had been issued as a United Nations unit, according to them one of our problems was that we could use weapons only for self-defence. Those rules were no longer in force and we returned to the rules governing the engagement of troops in combat." And in lines 23 to 25, he says the following, and I quote: "Since the issuance of the green order, we were in combat with the VRS, with the Army of Republika Srpska. The Army of Republika Srpska was a target for us and vice versa and that was realistic and true." And on page 3484, lines 1 to 3, he says the following, and I quote, and I'm quoting Colonel Franken: "My mandate changed substantially since the moment when the United Nations issued the order to me to defend Srebrenica. That was the reason why I issued the green order. Following that rule of engagement, et cetera, all restrictions on the use of weapons were lifted because that is consonant with an order to defend something." Thank you. My question is: If all the rules as Mr. Franken states had been revoked following the issuance of the green order, had such rules also been eliminated in respect of the Army of Republika Srpska also if they had been lifted in respect of UNPROFOR troops? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds like an excellent question for Colonel Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But did he tell you, you who were in combat, that all rules had been cancelled by the very issuance of the green order and by engaging in combat with the VRS and that now, or from that point on, you had to act in accordance with the green order rules?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that order, as I mentioned earlier. All I said was that, should we be in a position to stop the advance of the Bosnian Serb tanks, we should about accordingly. Still, I was instructed to draw a hypothetical line there and I did so. And that's what I have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that you had been ordered, that for you, as Mr. Franken, your superior states here, that you had been ordered that the VRS would be your target and you would be -- were their target, did you then have to adapt on the ground, your conduct on the ground, to the rules of combat of rules of engagement, combat with an enemy?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no. We were still driving in our white vehicles. We still wore our blue helmets. We were still positioned in the middle of the road until on July 10th, 1995, a tank fired at me. And I took up a position elsewhere. Nothing changed for me. The bearing of the arms was 800 metres. I didn't have any anti-tank shells with me -- excuse me, the range of the arms was 800 metres. All I could do was speak with aeroplanes if there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you comported yourselves as if you were still members of UNPROFOR, you wore blue helmets, you were in white vehicles, et cetera. But if you had been issued a green order to open fire on the Army of Republika Srpska, as Colonel Franken says, didn't that mean that in self-defence the Army of Republika Srpska would return fire, would also open fire at you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what I could have used to shoot at tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But why did you go to a position where you were in full sight of the VRS, as you say in paragraph 5? Why did you leave your shelter and went there where you would be in their full sight? Can you explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I remember that that was very well explained by the witness why he was visible at that point. I think half an hour ago he explained that in detail.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge. Then I shall rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you place yourself in full sight of the VRS in order for them to open fire at you as you were already at war with them, and was the order that you received such that you were to provoke fire on the part of the VRS by placing yourselves in that position?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not at war with the VRS at that moment. That's what you're referring to. I received my orders at that moment from Captain Groen, and he told me to return to that position to indicate to them, and by "them," I mean the VRS, that a line was drawn on the map that they were not supposed to cross. That's why I was standing there with my vehicle. When we talk about this 15 years afterwards, I understand clearly that we were very, very fortunate that we were not hit head-on with the tens of soldiers being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say here, now, was it maybe foolish from a soldierly aspect to place ones self in a position which is unsheltered, unprotected, and which is in full sight of the other side's fire?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If my instructions were to destroy the Bosnian Serb army, or, in any case, to make such an attempt, I would have acted differently. In this case, my instructions were to return to that blocking position to indicate clearly to the Bosnian Serb army that UNPROFOR was there, would remain there, and that there was a line that they were not allowed to cross. If I had thought green, as you're describing, then we would have acted differently. And I would not have positioned myself in the middle of the road, wearing a blue helmet in a white vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that ten minutes later you came under mortar and tank fire. Then in paragraph 5 you say: "The escape route also came under fire; however, we returned to a safe place. Our vehicle was hit several times." Why did you return to your safe place if everything was the way you have just explained to us?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was aware that it was not safe to return. Still, I was explicitly instructed to return to make clear that we were staying there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is time for our first break. Before we do that, I have to give the floor to the Registrar to assign an exhibit number to document 65 ter 3484. We are dealing with that at the outset of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This will be Exhibit P1304.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Marked for identification, pending translation. We adjourn and resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, I was told that it was not quite clear in the transcript where this marketplace that you spoke about was in Srebrenica. Where exactly near your base was it, how far was that marketplace from your base, or how far was your base from that marketplace, if you would be so kind to tell us?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. There was a marketplace in the city itself, in the city of Srebrenica, about 1 kilometre from the compound of the Bravo Company, that was also the UNHCR's storage site. Have I explained that sufficiently that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. How far was that in kilometres from the position which you took up on the road where you charted the -- what you referred to as the hypothetical line?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at blocking position 1 at that moment en route from Srebrenica to Observation Post Alpha in a hairpin turn, perhaps 2 kilometres, but I would have to check that on the map, from the position. In any case, the road went sharply upward. On the map it looks closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, but please tell us how far was that from your base in Srebrenica in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica we had the Bravo Company compound, and it would probably be 2, perhaps 3 kilometres - again, I would have to check that on the map - away from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We should take a look at page 3 of your statement. We shall take a look at the last paragraph on page 3 where you refer to the aircraft attack on VRS tanks. You say, and I quote: "The Dutch F-16s, they knocked two Bosnian Serbian tanks out of action. This made it possible for us to return to the compound of the Bravo Company in Srebrenica." Thank you: "At that moment there were dozens of people on the road in Srebrenica. We directed them towards Potocari. Chaos reigned," et cetera. My question is: Bearing in mind what you say here, who actually showed the target to these aircraft, who on the ground actually pointed the targets to the aircraft?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forward air controllers did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not receive a translation. Thank you. Were the forward air controllers in the vehicle which you placed on the road and which flew a white flag, this armoured personnel carrier that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that moment I had one forward air controller on my crew, but he was difficult to deploy, and from different positions others guided the F-16s to the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were -- where were these different positions that from which the aircraft were guided to the Serbian tanks?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One position was with me, we included this in the net, and two other commands -- commandos did this from a position that at the time was not visible to me. I couldn't point it out on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise to the Defence. Witness, I have a question for you. I would like you to clarify something that I didn't quite understand. On page 32 of today's transcript, line 11, that's where your witness statement is quoted and you are talking about an F-16, about the Dutch -- the Dutch F-16, which destroyed two Serb tanks. Did that F-16 belong to the Dutch Battalion or to UNPROFOR or to NATO? Could you please clarify this distinction and let's look at the command chain in that military structure that was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps a misinterpretation. Judge Mindua was referring to page 30 and not 32. Now, please answer this question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The F-16 that was deployed was a NATO F-16. Coincidentally, it was a Dutch F-16. And this makes communicating in Dutch between the pilot and the people on the ground much easier, but the -- it was a NATO F-16 that was deployed. It could have been a different F-16 or a different fighter plane. Ordinarily, we communicate with them in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank Judge Mindua for clarifying this very significant issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether the communication between the Dutch soldiers who were on their positions and the F-16 aircraft was exclusively in Dutch? Did they communicate in Dutch or in English? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened in with the forward air controller at my position, and he started in Dutch -- excuse me, he started in English and subsequently spoke in Dutch with the pilot. There may be audio recordings of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It is true that there is an audio recording. Do you remember the contents of their communications, if you remember, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did NATO get involved as a third party in the conflict between the Serbs and the Muslims when they opened fire on the positions of the VRS? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I understand is that the concept of the safe area of Srebrenica could not exist without the airforce. We were very poorly armed, could not shoot at anything, and all we could do was to request close air support. That was an essential element of the concept. When we were fired at in the enclave, we asked -- we requested that air support via the line. The battalion did that. It was not done by me on the ground. I was fired at and I reported that. Afterwards, F-16s arrived, and I'll leave it at that. That's what I can state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether on the 11th of July a massive air-strike or a massive air support was expected? Were there rumors that all targets are -- 1 kilometre around Srebrenica would be destroyed by those air-strikes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was promised many, many times that air support would arrive, and I prepared for that. All I saw were the F-16s. There was a rumor that there would be more air support from larger planes, but they were never seen and they never flew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statement you said that you had never received the expected air support. Did you have in mind the large-scale air support when you said that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about any type of air support. The only thing that came was at the very last moment two F-16s, and that was far too little and far too late to stop the Serb advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether you heard that Colonel Karremans had informed both the Muslims and your officers alike that there would be an air support that destroy all targets within an area of 1 square kilometre around Srebrenica? Did you ever hear of any such thing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was said that a gun-ship would arrive that would neutralise armoured targets in the south of the enclave; however, that was never carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now tell us this: Those aircrafts that would have arrived on that gun-ship, were they on the strength of UNPROFOR or on the strength of NATO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned a gun-ship, it was explained to me that that was an aeroplane, a gun-ship from which armoured vehicles could be destroyed. Because UNPROFOR units were being fired at, we could expect air support, close air support, or other forms of action from the air. How it was organised above me, UNPROFOR or NATO, I have no idea. What I do know is that we stood there waiting, helplessly, were fired at multiple times waiting for air support that never arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR have aeroplane carriers on its strength that could undertake a number of sorties and that could destroy an area of 1 square kilometre around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know and I still don't know whether UNPROFOR had its own combat planes. That didn't matter to me. We were promised that if we were fired at on the ground support would be provided from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the engagement of NATO and aeroplane carriers, was that a air support or a large-scale use of NATO airforce?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say in response to this question is that after repeated reports by us on the ground in blocking position 1, two F-16s appeared on the horizon. That's the only thing that was deployed. So there was no massive deployment of multiple planes, only two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are talking about announcements that you would be supported by an aeroplane carrier, and if that had materialised, if an aeroplane carrier had been engaged, you're a colonel, you certainly know what an aeroplane carrier has on it. So if such a device had, indeed, been deployed, would that constitute an air support or a large-scale attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't quarrel, I think, with the gist of General Tolimir's question, but there may be a translation problem that's complicating matters. I don't know how this term "gun-ship" is getting translated to General Tolimir. I think the witness tried to explain that he was referring to a single aeroplane with the capability of destroying multiple armoured targets. That is my understanding, and I think we are all agreed, that that is how Colonel Egbers defined his use of the term "gun-ship," because in his response to his first use of that term as we saw it, General Tolimir began speaking about what I think he may have perceived to be aircraft carriers which we all know are deployed at sea. Now, if, in fact, General Tolimir is referring to aircraft carriers, we have no problem with him asking those kind of questions. I think the Trial Chamber has already heard testimony from a couple of witnesses and will hear more testimony from other witnesses, such as General Smith, about NATO's capabilities, about the fact that aircraft carriers were available to NATO, among other resources. But I sense that there may be some speaking at cross-purposes presently where General Tolimir is insisting on this idea of aeroplane carriers and insisting that Colonel Egbers has been referring to aeroplane carriers or aircraft carriers. I think the transcript could bear some clarification on that point before we go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, you could perhaps help everybody by telling us what is your understanding of the word "aircraft carrier" and of the word "gun-ship"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be happy to. I never used the word "aircraft carrier." I did use the word "gun-ship." And in 1995, I was told that that was an aeroplane, not an F-16, but a large plane from which armoured vehicles, tanks, could be destroyed. So it's a single aeroplane that would fly over the enclave. I am not referring to massive actions and massive planes. And what, in fact, came were two F-16s. I hope that it's sufficiently clear that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should carry on your examination. My problem with the last question before the intervention of Mr. Thayer was that it is really a hypothetical question, and I am not sure if this witness is in the position to explain what your understanding could be or the understanding of those who are in the position to order such an action by aircraft. But you have received an answer from this witness what happened on the ground from his point of view.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am not interested in who could have issued that order. I am only interested in who was it who informed UNPROFOR that there would be a large-scale use of a NATO airforce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could the witness please answer, who was it who informed them that a large-scale NATO airforce exercise would be carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would prefer to receive, first, the affirmation by the witness if he got information that there would be a large-scale NATO airforce exercise. Did you, at that time, receive such an information and, if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive that at that time. All we did was report that we were being fired at, that there was a tank at a maximum of 2 kilometres distance firing at us, and subsequently two F-16s arrived and contacted our forward air controllers and tried to neutralise that tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, I asked you if you had heard that a large-scale NATO operation was announced for the 11th and that Colonel Karremans told both the Muslims and the UNPROFOR that an area of 1 square kilometre around Srebrenica would be destroyed and that he demanded the withdrawal of certain forces. And did that also apply to UNPROFOR forces? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that there was a NATO exercise, an exercise of NATO aeroplanes in 1995 in the area of Srebrenica. All I was told was that a large aeroplane might come that could destroy armoured vehicles and tanks. That large aeroplane never arrived. All that came were two F-16s.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I understood your question and I proceed. If that large plane had, perchance, arrived and destroyed all those targets around Srebrenica, would that be -- would that have been a large-scale NATO operation or would that have been close air support for the forces that had come under threat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to give an answer about a situation that never took place. I don't even know whether we have such a plane in the air. All I obtained was close air support, and you need to ask such questions at your own level, to generals, who do indeed take those actual decisions. I was standing on the ground, I was fired at and reported that to my captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egbers. You were on the ground. Did you receive instruction to leave such an area that would be a designated target because such instruction was provided to the Muslims, and Captain Egbers [as interpreted] said that the ship returned, and so on and so forth. I could quote him if you wish. I am just asking if you received an order to withdraw from the area that was designated as the target of an attack and did the Muslims also withdraw from that area? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only at blocking position 1. I was at the market in the city of Srebrenica, and I was never south of that hypothetical line. I was on that line, so I was never removed from an area south of Bravo 1. So I cannot give you an answer that is any different from this one. I don't know - because you're suggesting that - I don't know that Muslims had to withdraw from a certain area. I don't know whether that happened. You would have to ask Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egbers. We will ask him when he comes to testify. But you should know this. Did you know on the 10th that the Muslims had left and had gone through the forest? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in contact with the Bosnian Muslims in the enclave at that time. I was on the market in the city and later in blocking position 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at page 3, in the statement that is on your screen now, line 14 which is the last line in the Serbian translation where it says -- or, rather, you say, and I am quoting your words: "Many people had already been -- had already fled through the forest in the direction of Tuzla." That will be on the next page in English. Thank you, Aleksandar. You can see the first paragraph in English where it says "of Tuzla." That's the activity which took place on the 10th, an activity that you speak about. In the next paragraph, you already speak about the 11th. I repeat my question: Did you learn from somebody, did you hear from somebody on the 10th that many people had already fled through the forest, through the woods, in the direction of Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement was drafted in October 1995, sometime after I had returned from the enclave. Then additional information was available that is also set forth in writing, but at that moment when I was there I did not know that large groups of men were gathering in the north-west of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I would note for the record, and I think we can save a little bit of time, or at least I hope we can, that the portion of the witness statement from which General Tolimir just quoted is part of the witness statement that deals with events that occurred on 11 July. And there, again, is no dispute among any of the parties that the close air support about which Colonel Egbers has been testifying at some length now occurred on 11 July. That is not nor can it reasonably be placed in dispute. It is a matter of historical record and I do not think that the Defence is disputing that part of the Prosecution's case. And if we look at the statement, the events that are described in the paragraph from which General Tolimir just quoted all concern events on 11 July: The F-16s arriving, the F-16s taking out the VRS tanks, the witness returning to Potocari, the column of civilians fleeing from -- pardon me, from Srebrenica to Potocari, that is all happening on the 11th of July and there is no dispute between the parties among that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge. We shall now ask the witness a very simple question without any suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does he know when the Dutch F-16 actually opened fire on the two tanks? Was that on the 10th or on the 11th of July? I shall repeat my question: When did the Dutch F-16 fire at the two tanks of the VRS, was it on the 10th or on the 11th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you state in your statement that it was on the 10th as you said and that you wrote it immediately after the event?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have such a horrible experience involving many, many emotions, it's difficult to pin-point it on a time chart. I don't have any notes as to when that happened. Later on in an interrogation you start reconstructing it for yourself when exactly -- what happened. And let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you that the refugees gathered, the women, children, old men, and young boys at the Bravo Company, the F-16s arrived, carried out their attack. That's why I was able to proceed to the Bravo Company, together with thousands of men, women, and children, to proceed from Srebrenica to Potocari to receive the refugees there. That happened in succession and I've stated about that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 of the statement in Serbian, paragraph 4, where the witness says, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give us the reference -- please give us the reference on the English page as well, for the sake of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's paragraph 4 in Serbian and paragraph 5 in the English version, on the previous page relative to the one that we now have on the screen. Because here he follows a chronology. Thank you. It is the third paragraph from the top where it is stated the 10th of July, 1995, and it also says the next day. There the witness describes events which took place on the 10th of July, and he does so until all the way into the next page up to the events which transpired on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Is this statement incorrect relative to the events that you are talking about here or is there a possibility that it might have been otherwise? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, and I stand by that, perhaps the date is indicated incorrectly here but the attack of the F-16s was on the date that we proceeded from Srebrenica to Potocari. Several times before that we were promised air support and that never arrived. So are you concerned about the date or the events?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to the next page where events were described which took place on the 11th and 12th. Thank you. Can you see where it is stated: "On Tuesday 11 July 1995 ..." It is the second paragraph in English, and it is also the second paragraph on page 4 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is -- or was whether the events of the 11th have been faithfully recorded or reflected in the witness's statement or not? In which case my question would be superfluous. My question is: Did you, on the 11th, on Tuesday the 11th of July, help refugees to the base?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 11 July, 1995, we proceeded from Srebrenica with thousands of men and women to Potocari and they were received at the DutchBat headquarters. Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: On the 11th of July, did you help the refugees at the base and at what time were you engaged on that task?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that thousands of people were in Srebrenica were unable to move one way or another. They were fired at in the south. Our entire column walked 5 kilometres to the north. In the afternoon it was about 35 degrees centigrade. I saw old men pushing forward their old wives in a wheelbarrow, I was given a baby by a mother asking if I would take care of the baby. I saw total panic and everybody was climbing over everything. I was given the sick and the injured from the hospital, and together we proceeded from Srebrenica to Potocari. And I drove near the front of that column, and I dropped off all the sick and injured that afternoon, at the hospital that afternoon. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you say that on the 10th in the evening around 1700 hours you dropped off the wounded to the first aid station at the base in Potocari. Is this statement of yours incorrect in terms of the date?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this happened on the 11th, and it does, indeed, appear incorrectly in the statement and that's unfortunate. But the events that I described obviously did take place. The attack by the F-16s and the flight of the women and children and older men from Srebrenica to Potocari took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether on Wednesday, the 12th of July, 1995, you received an order to help evacuate the refugees as you state on page 4, paragraph 3, line 1? You can also see it on the screen where it is dated Wednesday, the 12th of July. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that I escorted the very first convoy of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's not what I asked. I asked whether it was on the 12th that you escorted refugees and whether it was a Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day after the attack on the enclave we escorted the first columns with buses. The first column with buses I escorted that, whether you are asking what time it was on Wednesday or was it on the 12th, do you have a substantive question about how that happened or are you trying to carry over the aforementioned error in the time-line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, do you recall the date when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that it was Wednesday the 12th, but I could check this in previous and different testimonies if the -- if General Tolimir wants me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason I rose a moment was, and hopefully again we can save a little bit of time. The witness testified very clearly about all of this subject matter and the dates in his prior testimony in the Popovic case at transcript page 2716 to 2719. All the events that are contained in this paragraph that was unfortunately not properly dated, all the events that are described in the subsequent paragraph, and all the events that are described in this paragraph that General Tolimir is currently questioning him on. It is all described in his prior testimony, transcript page 2716 to 2719.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, it is really of no consequence to me on what date it was or whether it was a mistake or not. What matters to me is to actually correlate the events that you are talking about with the participants in those events. As we cannot speak about exact dates, I will ask you this: You say here that on the 12th, as you say, you follow the route which was taken by the refugees, the road taken by them, you follow the buses, that one bus broke down, and that a Serb officer helped you gets the refugees off this bus that had broken down and into a bus in good repair. And then you go on to say that you were stopped, you were intercepted in the evening, that you had to spend the night at a school where there was a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska, that Muslims actually broke through the woods and that you saw a number of captured Muslims and that they opened fire at the school in which you spent the night. Did all these events that you describe happen on -- in the night between the 12th and the 13th? Did all these events happen that you describe in your statement on page 4 as having happened on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very -- I escorted the very first transport of refugees. I drove via Bratunac to Kladanj, and every hundred metres I tried to maintain contact with UNPROFOR to report where we were going. I stated earlier about unloading the buses, and I've stated earlier that that evening I drove back to Srebrenica again. The next day I received instructions to escort another transport of refugees. I've told you that men were separated from women, that I was in the house with the men, that I told the men that they would be going to a Muslim area as well, and, later on, with that transport 4 once again, via Bratunac, I drove to Kladanj again. Along my return, I was stopped at Nova Kasaba. Have I given you a better chronological account of what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order for us to establish what happened on the 12th and what on the 13th, I will read page 4, paragraph 6, that's lines 1 to 3 in Serbian and in English it is page 5, the first paragraph. In fact, it is the last paragraph that we now see in English. I apologise. Actually, now it is the first one. "There were more buses near Kladanj. Refugees got out at the stop, three buses at a time. From this point they were allowed to walk to freedom. I saw some ten Bosnian Serbs at the stop, but I did not see them treat anybody badly." Then it goes on to say: "I stayed at Kladanj for an hour or so, then I went back with Lutke and another vehicle followed. I radioed in saying that there the refugees were still sitting in the football field in Nova Kasaba. The situation along the road remained unchanged."
