Tell me, does this refer to the first day of evacuation, the 12th of July, and was that the end of July, the 12th?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the first day of the evacuation at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 5, the first paragraph in line 1, that is in the Serbian, you say that: "... on Thursday, the 13th of July, 1995, I had to report to Captain Melchers at 0600." My question is: Was that the beginning of the 13th of July, in terms of your activities for that day?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was indeed on the second day I was escorting convoys, and I was expected to report to Captain Melchers at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us who this captain was and was he a member of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was indeed a Dutch UNPROFOR captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 1 you described how you went to the house where men were separated from the women to check out the situation, and so on and so forth. We shall now move on to paragraph 3, on page 5, to look at lines 10 from 14 which I shall quote. In fact, just the penultimate and the ultimate lines, 13 and 14. You say that you saw a black Volkswagon and a man in black: "And I asked him whether he could stop an empty bus for me so that we could actually take the refugees in them and he did so, and I took that bus to Kladanj." My question is: Was that the last bus that you dispatched to Kladanj on that 13th of July or were there any others or any other activities following that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second day I escorted convoys, I did not see a black but a red Volkswagon with a colonel on board who was able to help me arrange a different bus to replace a bus that broke down. Presumably, the bus had broken down and something else had to be arranged for those people. I drove behind that bus up to Kladanj. Does that answer your question sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Was this the last day that you escorted refugees or sent the refugees to Kladanj, since later refer to being stopped together with Captain Lutke, if I am right?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the return journey from Kladanj I was stopped at Nova Kasaba by a roadblock. A gun was pointed at me, and I had to surrender my vehicle. And you mentioned Captain Lutke but it was Sergeant Lutke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, on page 47, line 22 and 23, you were recorded to have said: "You say that you saw a black Volkswagon and a man in black." The witness answered that he didn't refer to a black but to a red Volkswagon, and just for the sake of the record I would like to note in the document on the screen we can see there, and I quote: "Shortly thereafter, a red Volkswagon wagon stopped. A man dressed entirely in a black uniform got out." Just to clarify the situation about the colours. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question: On the 12th and the 13th, these last two days when you escorted this column to Kladanj, did you take to Kladanj all the people that you had actually taken in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with Major Franken about the escorts for the buses. He wanted to have an UNPROFOR soldier on each bus. He told me that that was prohibited by the Bosnian Serbs. The very first convoy of buses was escorted by UNPROFOR from the front and the rear, that was allowed, but later on only by a vehicle that would drive behind the buses. Transport 3, which transported the men from the white house, according to Lieutenant Versteeg, did not arrive in Kladanj. The two transports of women and children I escorted were, as far as I saw, they did arrive in Kladanj. Later, when I was detained in Nova Kasaba in the school, all buses rode without escorts, and I can't say anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about these first two days, whether all the buses transported all the people and came back up to the point when you were stopped. Did the buses return to Srebrenica in order to continue with the evacuation on the next day as well, the third day? And I'm not mentioning any dates because of the chronology which is lacking in your statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a brief answer. On the two days that I performed these escorting duties, the first day, the very first transport, something happened to one of the buses. One of those buses was broken down by the side of the road. I talked about that. When a replacement bus arrived, I drove behind that bus to Kladanj. All other buses were there and the people alighted, and then I drove back in my vehicle along the football field in Nova Kasaba back to the compound in Srebrenica. The next day the transport with men was number 3. They were not escorted. I did the fourth transport. These buses arrived in Kladanj. I drove back in the direction of Potocari but was stopped at the school of Nova Kasaba. Does this answer your question sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Is there a written report on behalf of UNPROFOR soldiers who escorted convoys from Srebrenica to Kladanj? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately upon my return from the school of Nova Kasaba where I spent the night with my 12 colleagues, I compiled an internal report and I presented that to the head of the section 2/3 as entered here yesterday. There were no instructions regarding escorting the buses. The situation was as follows: We saw all those people standing and waiting in the burning Sunday, and all of a sudden 12 buses showed up from Zvornik and other places, and we were expected to follow them. I didn't even know where those buses were headed. I couldn't tell those people what was going to happen with them and where they would be brought, so there were no written instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did those people know where they were going? They knew the area, they were familiar with the communications, did they know where they were going? Did they ask you where they were going?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they wanted to know, and they asked me, but I didn't know. Only the bus drivers knew where they were going. Not until the second day could I tell them that I had been near Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether those people who attended the meeting on the 12th at the Fontana Hotel, did they make arrangements as to where those people would be taken? Did they know where they would be taken, and did they inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Those who transported the people, were they supposed to tell every UNPROFOR soldier what was going on, or were they only supposed to convey that to Karremans and depend on him to inform his soldiers what to do? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the captain that you just mentioned. He was instructed to assign the transport on the first day, and he told me, that's Captain Melchers, he told me that he didn't know where the transports were headed. I -- in any case, I had to bring enough food, drink, and sleeping bags along.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you didn't know what had been agreed by the representatives of the Muslim community and the representatives of the VRS about that evacuation? Please answer by just saying yes or no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say yes or no to that because I don't know whether -- I don't know whether those agreements were reached, all I can say is that I didn't know that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you answered Mr. Thayer's question and you spoke about a woman who had died on one of the buses and you spoke about the others leaving the bus and walking through the forest. Bearing in mind what had happened, was that a forcible death or was the death of that woman the result of the temperatures, the high temperatures in the bus and the heat on the bus?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to guess what the cause of death was, and I am not in a position to do that. All I can say is what I observed, and I described to you yesterday what the conditions were and what the temperature was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Also you told us yesterday that the others had been chased out of the bus and that they had been forced to walk through the woods. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that others were chased out of the bus. In fact, it was very orderly. The buses were all stationary. The first three buses drove up, the doors opened, and people were allowed to walk down a certain road. Once those buses were empty the next ones arrived and the ones after them. They didn't know exactly where they were walking, and later on it turned out that they were walking to the Muslim area of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for the explanation. Thank you for clarifying the situation for us. And now could you answer another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce Exhibit P1143. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The document describes a situation on the 13th of July, Thursday, as you say, in Nova Kasaba. Some of the people were loaded on the busses and left in the direction of Tuzla. I am going to read from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 18 in English and 27 in Serbian. The paragraph number is 287. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We will see the paragraph shortly. The paragraph is 287. Now we see it on the screen. You say this: "No." And I quote, I quote what you said: "No. But one thing about Nova Kasaba is mentioned. I have it here before me. It says, 'Thursday, 13 July, at least one of the convoys was stopped at the football field in the surroundings of Nova Kasaba. The Army of Bosnian Serbs,'" as you call it, "'set up a place there where able-bodied men were gathered. A number of men were allowed to get on the buses and they were transferred to Kladanj.'" "Yes." And now I'm reading from paragraph 288: "Yes. That was another convoy. I was not with it. But I did indeed hear that -- the story that some men were allowed to get on the buses. Maybe they were friends or acquaintances or something like that." My question is this: In these two paragraphs, 287 and 288, you speak about a certain number of people who had gathered in Nova Kasaba who were allowed to board the buses and leave for Tuzla. Do you have any more information about the stories that you had heard? Can you tell us how many people boarded the buses, and so on and so forth? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you see, the question under paragraph 287 appears in italics. This was information from the investigator of the Dutch Institute for War Documentation. He probably obtained that information elsewhere and was asking whether I can tell him anything about that. In 1999 when this report was drafted, all I could say was that I had heard about it at the time but that I was not present there. All I can say is that that didn't happen on my transports. I can't tell you anything more about that. What I say, starting with maybe, is, of course, an interpretation of an interview question because you start thinking about what could possibly be the reason. In retrospect, that's an awkward addition. It would have been better for me to say that I didn't personally experience that, only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to complete this information, bearing in mind what the Dutch institute asked you, let's look at paragraph 292 where you say: "No. Yes. Precisely so. When we stopped by the burning bus, you could see also that the Muslims and the Serbs who had lived together for a number of years before that and knew each other and were still on friendly terms. They hugged each other. I can very well imagine. It was a state of chaos. And I can very well imagine somebody stopping buses and crying, 'These Muslims have to stay alive.' And that's quite possible." And now let me quote the other paragraphs, but before that did I quote the Dutch investigator's words correctly? Did I quote their question correctly? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What I take from this document is that was the answer of the witness and not the question by the Dutch representative. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, Mr. President. And just to follow-up on Colonel Egbers's previous answer, he tried it himself and said that perhaps his answer was a little clumsy. But if General Tolimir is going to be quoting from this document then I think the record should reflect that, in fact, the following question at 289, paragraph 289, is: "Yes." 1 And Colonel Egbers responds: "But I wouldn't know who did that." Which I think is precisely what Colonel Egbers was trying to communicate in his last answer. And then furthermore, in fact, General Tolimir did not read the question at paragraph 291 into the record. He simply quoted Colonel Egbers's answer. And the question is, from the NIOD interviewer: "I don't know who reported that either, but I found that really remarkable."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And now your next question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since I've been asked to read everything, let me read paragraph 296, the last one on page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says here: "Yes, but in the beginning there was no selection. In the beginning they let everybody in. Only later did they start to select people. On the second day." My question is this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Honestly, this is atrocious. General Tolimir well knows that the next question, if we turn the next page in English, paragraph 297, is: "It really only started on the second day." And the witness's answer is: "Yes, as far as I know. Don't hold me to that. I wasn't there." And I just point that out for the record to save a little bit of time in potential redirect because this is nonsense and it's misleading cross-examination. General Tolimir just claimed that he was being forced to read all of the paragraphs, and we will require him to place these paragraphs in the fair and accurate context in which they should be placed by an Officer of the Court, in this case, a self-represented accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you shall take that into consideration, but we have our second break now and we will resume at quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 2906, lines 15 to 20 from Popovic case, it says and I quote: "Q. Were you taken hostage by the Muslims while you were in the enclave?" Your answer to that was this, and I quote: "I was in the Bandera Triangle when we entered the enclave in January 1995." I'll skip a few questions because they are illegible, and now it says, and I quote, the question by the Defence: "Is it fair to say that the person who took you hostage was under the command of a person called Zulfo?" And your answer was this: "That's correct. That's what I was told. "Q. Muslim forces under Zulfo's command, were they responsible for the area between observation posts Alpha and Charlie?" Your answer was this: "That was something that we thought, that Zulfo was one who was superior to those who were he in the enclave." My question, based on what I have just quoted, is this, and the question is to you, sir -- I have just been informed that something was mis-recorded: "You said that's what I was told, that Zulfo was in charge of the men who were in that part of the enclave." I apologise to the interpreters for speeding up. I believe that that was the cause of the error. My question to you, sir, is this: Zulfo, who is referred to in here in this transcript, is that Zulfo Tursunovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reading out your -- reading out the statement, there is another small error. In -- I hear that in July 1995 I was in the Bandera Triangle, but now once again were you talking about a time at the start of the enclave. Yesterday, at the request of the OTP I responded that upon entering, as a new Dutch battalion, we faced advancing Serbs. We are talking about the period January and February 1995 and not during the fall of the enclave. I was told that in that period, if that's what you mean, somebody named Zulfo was responsible for Muslim operations in that Bandera Triangle. I don't know his surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I take it that you quoted from the Popovic transcript, that was P1142. We have another document on the screen still and this is not the right one. I just wanted to make that clear for the record. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so the record is completely clear on this point. At page 2906, line 12, the witness's answer was, in fact: "I was at the Bandera Triangle in the west of the enclave as we entered the enclave in January 1995." That was the witness's answer in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank everybody for supplementing. I would not waste anymore time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My next question is this: Did the OTP ask you to recognise this man, Zulfo, who is referred to herein? Did they ask you to recognise him in a photo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why were you taken as hostage in January 1995 in the Bandera Triangle? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, we were denied access to that triangle on the argument that we were not acting as UNPROFOR against the Serbs or Bosnian Serbs, that with each new battalion commander took away a section of the enclave, according the view of the Muslims. In January 1995 in the surroundings west of the enclave, known as the Bandera Triangle, that was said to be the case. There the Serbs were said to have advanced in the direction of the enclave without any action by UNPROFOR. When we entered that triangle nonetheless, in our vehicles, the roads were blocked by the Muslims. Does that answer your question sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you've answered my question. We know that UNPROFOR's movements were restricted in the Bandera Triangle. Did UNPROFOR react to that? Did they announce that there would be air-strikes because of that? Did they ever say that to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we were not fired at, the roads were blocked and the rank of the battalion of Major Franken led this operation to enter that area, nonetheless, with UNPROFOR troops. At that level, negotiations were conducted with representatives of the Bosnian Muslims who lived in the enclave, and those negotiations led to restoring freedom of movement for the Dutch groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if UNPROFOR informed Serbs about the restriction on their movements in the so-called Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told later that the observers were in contact with the Bosnian Serbs and spoke about this in Bratunac, but at the time I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did UNPROFOR ever try to secure the freedom of movement in the zone demilitarised according to the agreement with the help of one of the sides that were guarantors to that agreement, and that was the Serbian side? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that happened. All I know is that there were UN observers and they spoke with both the Muslims and the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the Popovic case on page 2907, lines 14 through 17, you speak about Zulfo Tursunovic, the organisation that he had established in the Bandera Triangle area, and about him as a person, that everybody was afraid of. My question is this: Did you see Zulfo Tursunovic after the events in the Bandera Triangle? Did you see him in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see Zulfo later, either in Srebrenica or while discharging your tasks?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to get back to the surname that you use in line 16, Tursunovic, you make it appear as if I mention that name in the Popovic case. Well, I just explained that I don't know that surname. And as I re-read lines 14 through 17, the surname doesn't appear there. But let me tell you which stories were being told about Zulfo. At the time we heard that he was said to be a criminal. He may have served time in prison. Those were the stories we heard, a criminal. I did not meet him. Are we talking about the same Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are talking about the same Zulfo. I refer to the surname for the transcript. Was he in prison whilst -- while UNPROFOR was -- [B/C/S spoken on English channel] Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise. Obviously some of the interpreters have not switched off their microphones in some of the booths so that we have some strange input in our earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was Zulfo, on account of his criminal activities, in prison before the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is that there was a rumor, and I don't know whether it was true, but rumor had it that he was said to have served time in prison before the war. During his stay in the enclave, there was no prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please tell us whether the UNPROFOR command demanded from the Muslim political leadership for the military commanders who were organising the army in the enclave to leave the enclave as a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please reformulate this question more clearly so that I know exactly what you mean, because I have read this twice now and I don't understand exactly what you want from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the UNPROFOR command ask the military Muslim -- I mean the political leadership of the Muslims in Sarajevo and Srebrenica that any of the military commanders leave the enclave on account of activities which were in contravention of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You would need to ask the UNPROFOR generals who might have spoken with you about this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the agreement were not all military activities prohibited in the Srebrenica enclave, was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is what I saw in the enclave. I did not observe any military activities except that the weapons were allowed to be maintained in the weapon collection point. I don't know -- I don't understand exactly which activities you mean that would not be prohibited in the enclave. Could you perhaps clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you meet with military representatives in the enclave or did other officers of the UNPROFOR meet with them or liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Naser Oric was in the enclave. He called himself a commander. Ramiz was there. He held a military rank as well. And locally in the area of Observation Post Alpha, I was in contact with a local authority, somebody who spoke on behalf of the people. But I was not in contact with other superior military representatives or liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have called up in e-court D66. Until it is brought up on the screen, I should say that it is a document which Naser Oric signed as his report which he dispatched to Tuzla and the chief of the General staff to Enver Hadzihasanovic, a brigade general. We now see it on the screen in the Serbian. I believe it is there now in the English as well, yes it is. I shall now quote a portion of this report which was sent on the 28th of January, 1995, to the addressees indicated in Kakanj and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote: "Due to the situations in the area of Podgaj village on 9 January 1995 of which you were informed in a timely manner, the command of the 8th Operations Group has restricted the movement of the -- of UNPROFOR forces in the wider region of Suceska and Podgaj. "At about 1100 hours today, the commander of the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica ordered his patrols to enter the movement restriction area. In co-ordination with the commander of the 8th Operations Group, respecting the agreement reached with the UNPROFOR liaison officer, after the warning was issued not to move in the aforementioned area, the commander of the 281st Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade blocked all UNPROFOR patrols and is still keeping them blocked. It was requested from the Dutch Battalion commander that this area be immediately visit by the UNPROFOR commander for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the representatives of the General Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the 2nd Corps command all with a view to finding a peaceful solution to the situation which has arisen in the Podgaj village sector and the General area of Suceska, i.e., the area of responsibility of the 281st Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade. "Please give us immediately instructions for further steps to be taken regarding UNPROFOR. "Commander Brigadier Naser Oric." My question is: It is obvious from this document that UNPROFOR had been issued a warning. It had been prohibited movement in the area of Bandera Triangle. My question is whether Enver or Evert Rave, who is referred to in this document, was the liaison officer at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is, because I have read this document together with you, you're asking whether there is a liaison. Can I find the same name in the document that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is not what I asked. But thank you for commenting on it. Was, at that time, Mr. Evert Rave the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the name should be Evert Rave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you mean -- the name Rave rings a bell. That's a colleague from UNPROFOR in the lower ranks and upper.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Wachtmeester," interpreter apologies, checking translation of "wachtmeester."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a sergeant-major. Whether he was the one who remained in contact with Naser Oric, I don't think so. I think it would have been Karremans's responsibility to maintain that contact, but all I can tell you is that I was there at that point and was unable to proceed. I've never seen that document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The document proposes that the commander of UNPROFOR for Bosnia and a representative of the General Staff; namely, a representative of the Army of the BH and the commander of the 2nd Corps should meet in order to bring about an early resolution to the situation, to the problem. Are you aware -- do you know that they indeed did meet in order to deal with the situation?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, not in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: From this document of Naser Oric that's sent to Tuzla and the General Staff, is it obvious that the Muslim army in Srebrenica was -- maintained an organised link with representatives of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that question directed at me or is that for the Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no right to ask the Judges. I put this question to you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I would have to interpret this document and, as I read this, it appears that there is a link between Naser Oric, the sender of this letter, and the General Staff to whom the letter is addressed. I can't say anything else about it. That was way above my level in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the Serbs knew or had been informed that the Muslims were prohibiting your movement in the Bandera Triangle area?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you earlier, I heard that our observers in Bratunac spoke about this with the Bosnian Serbs. I even believe I remember that the Bosnian Serbs offered their assistance, but I don't remember that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this restriction of movement, in a zone such as the Bandera Triangle was, was it -- sorry, I made a mistake. Was the prohibition on UNPROFOR's movement in a sector which was called the Bandera Triangle, was it contrary to the provisions of the demilitarisation agreement?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Muslims conduct any illegal activities in the Bandera Triangle that they did he not want UNPROFOR to be aware of, and, if so, and if you know that that was the case, can you tell us what it was?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no indications to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there exist a possibility that the Muslims did conduct any illegal prohibited activities there which representatives of UNPROFOR and UNPROFOR patrols were to have sanctioned?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The activities and shooting incidents were in the area of Observation Post Alpha, north of the triangle. We had patrols in the area and looked around the area with binoculars, but we had no reason to assume that other activities, illegal activities as you describe them, were taking place. Otherwise, I assume that the Bosnian Serbs would have notified our observers in Bratunac so that we would have been able to take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have frequently referred to observers in your answers. Did you mean UN observers in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina or UNPROFOR observers who were part of the Dutch battalion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our people who were regularly outside the enclave were the UN observers. We also had people from other countries, African nations carrying out these duties. I don't remember their names clearly, but I am sure they are in the file. They would leave the enclave and were in contact with both the Bosnian Serbs and with the Muslims in the enclave. You'll find them as UNMOs, United Nations Military Observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me whether at any time after that incident you had a right to move around the -- or within the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there after that and I don't know for certain whether other UNPROFOR soldiers were there later on, but I assume that Zulfo, in his section, did not allow the UNPROFOR patrols. I would have to check that in previous statements, but if you are asking me I was -- I did not go back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to disarm armed Muslims within so-called Zulfo's zone or brigade when you observed such -- any armed Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not there anymore because it was not in my company's sector. It was Captain Groen's area. I was responsible with my company for the northern part of the enclave, but when you can't get there you can't confiscate arms either, if that's the answer you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is the answer which I wanted. Colonel Franken certainly knew the answer to what I am interested in. In 1995 he was Karremans deputy. And in June 2010, on page 338 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot follow the speaker. He should slow down, please, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are much too fast again. The interpreters can't follow you. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was: Were you allowed to disarm Muslims when you found yourselves outside that zone, in any area outside Zulfo's zone?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were entitled to confiscate weapons from Muslims throughout the enclave and store them in the weapon collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you saw a Muslim going into a house and carrying weapons, were you entitled to follow him into that house?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that happened. I don't know specifically whether that was officially regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I shall quote what Mr. Franken said on the 30th of June, 2010, 3384, lines 12 to 15 of the transcript. And he said this, and I quote: "We had a minor problem. The moment we entered a house we were not authorised to enter that house, and we were to call the local police in order to search that house so that that was not very effective." My question is: Was this actually the practice, the procedure throughout the Srebrenica zone as described by Mr. Franken in what I have just quoted?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds like a good question for Major Franken. All I know is that special forces did go after the people, also into their house, to confiscate weapons. I understand based to Major Franken's statement that they weren't entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there's a correction necessary. On page 68, line 20, you quoted Mr. Franken in the following way, I quote: "We had a minor problem. The moment we enter the house." It should read, "They entered the house." Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am standing now just so we don't go over time too much. I just wanted to raise one proposal with the Trial Chamber and, frankly, with the witness. As I mentioned at the outset, we do not have the Dutch interpreters available for tomorrow, but I wanted to at least provide the alternative to Colonel Egbers, if he so chooses, and this is without any indication of any preference on the part of the Prosecution, because we have none with respect to this issue, for him to return tomorrow if he desires to testify in English. Obviously he has chosen to testify in Dutch, and we understand that, and again we have got no position. But if Colonel Egbers is available tomorrow and would prefer to get the completion of his testimony accomplished tomorrow, that is an option. Not a satisfactory one, I expect, but I just wanted to put that out there because the alternative is that he has to come back on another day when we can schedule the Dutch interpreters which, again, is fine with the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. I note that the cross-examination lasted up to now around four hours. Mr. Tolimir, you indicated earlier that you will need seven hours altogether. Can I take it that you need again three hours for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That is the time within which we could conclude with our questioning, given the situation that we are in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And before I ask the witness if he would be able to testify in English, I would like to know, Mr. Thayer, there is another witness from abroad scheduled for tomorrow and Thursday. Would that not cause another problem if we will continue with Mr. Egbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, my understanding from the Defence is that the best estimate is that that other witness's testimony can be completed in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are referring to Mr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that the case, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If that witness comes, we will finish him. And if Colonel agrees to come tomorrow, we will finish him as well. That's the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers, you have followed the discussion about the different options how to conclude your testimony. One is that you testify in English tomorrow for around three hours and some more time, or that you come back at a later day when the Dutch interpreters will be available. What is your position on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At previous trials I testified in English, but I often had to search for words. For example, when I explain that a man is pushing forward his wife in a wheelbarrow to Potocari, then I have to describe the word "wheelbarrow" which I don't often use in English. And now I can speak my own language, I am able to be clearer about what I mean, and I think that both Mr. Tolimir and the Prosecutor are best served by that. So I propose that we set a new date. I live in this country so I can come at short notice when interpreters are present. I think that this trial is too important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. I think this is a clear position we have received from the witness so that we have to conclude your testimony at another day, that will be discussed between the parties and you will get the invitation in due course. First of all, the Chamber has to thank you for your attendance yesterday and today, and we are sorry that you have to come back at a later stage. Please be reminded that it is not allowed to have contact to either party about the content of your testimony during the break. Thank you again. And we have to adjourn now and resume tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of November, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.06 p.m.,
